questions.prompt: A request: monthly tug fuel use per call, from one system, for an internal note that nobody acts on for at least a quarter. With the unit's matrix (effect by complexity) and its escalators, which level does it get?
options: Level 1: a low effect and a low complexity
Level 2: every analysis needs a second pair of eyes
Level 3: fuel is a cost, and costs go to the board
Level 2: the data come from an operational system
questions.explanation: An error in an internal note that changes nothing for a quarter has a low effect; one source and a routine method is low complexity, and no escalator applies.
misconceptions: Treats peer review as a minimum for all work, which spends review hours where an error does no harm
Grades the topic instead of the use: the note decides nothing
Takes the source system as a risk factor; the matrix asks what an error would change

questions.prompt: Two analysts grade the same request with your written standard. One gives level 2, the other level 3. Both used the matrix correctly. What does the difference most likely show?
options: One analyst is more careful than the other
A definition in the standard can be read two ways
The matrix has too few levels to be useful
The request should go to the head of unit to decide
questions.explanation: If both applied the matrix, they graded a factor differently, which means its definition admits two readings; tightening it is the fix.
misconceptions: Blames the person, when the standard's words allowed both readings
Adds levels, which multiplies the boundaries where readings differ
Escalates one case and leaves the ambiguous definition in place for the next

questions.prompt: In a unit of twelve, the analyst who built the berth demand model is also the most senior person free to assure it. Under the four roles, what should happen?
options: He assures it, since he knows the model best
He approves it, and a junior analyst assures it
Another senior assures it, even if that waits a week
The commissioner assures it, as the person who asked
questions.explanation: The assurer must be independent of the analyst; knowing the model best is exactly why he cannot see its blind spots.
misconceptions: Confuses expertise with independence: the author cannot assure his own work
Swaps the roles but keeps him signing off his own analysis
Gives assurance to the person who wants the answer, who is not independent of it

questions.prompt: You adapt a published 32-item checklist written for machine-learning studies. Most of the unit's work is counts and comparisons for directors. What is the best first step?
options: Adopt all 32 items as they stand, so that nothing the authors found is missed
Use it only for level 4 analyses
Replace it with one question: is the work reproducible?
Map the items to the review areas and keep those the unit's work needs
questions.explanation: Mapping shows which items serve the unit's areas and where nothing does (communication), so the checklist fits the work and gets used.
misconceptions: Assumes a longer checklist is safer, when reviewers skip what does not fit
Keeps the checks from the work that needs them most often
Collapses many checks into one that two reviewers would answer differently

questions.prompt: Which checklist item can two reviewers answer the same way?
options: Are excluded records counted, with a reason for each exclusion?
Is the analysis rigorous?
Is the data quality good enough?
Would an experienced expert in the field approve of the method used?
questions.explanation: It is a yes-or-no question that names its evidence (a count per exclusion step), so both reviewers look at the same thing.
misconceptions: Uses an adjective that each reviewer reads differently
Asks for a judgement with no named evidence, so each reviewer uses their own bar
Imports a hypothetical judge instead of something in the files

questions.prompt: A level 1 dashboard request is checked by its analyst. Which item must the self-check still include?
options: An independent re-run of the analysis from its repository
No personal data and the classification marked
An interval on every number
A second reviewer's severity ratings
questions.explanation: Leakage harms people whatever the level of the analysis, so the privacy and classification item applies from level 1.
misconceptions: An independent re-run is the cost that level 2 and above pay
Intervals matter where a decision depends on a number, from level 2
Second reviews belong to calibration and level 4, not a self-check

questions.prompt: A colleague's script runs to the end on your laptop and prints 5.18 days; the report says 4.60. Nothing failed. What do you do next?
options: Accept the report: the code ran without errors
Accept your figure and correct the report
Look for a step that happened outside the code
Average the two figures and note the range
questions.explanation: A gap with no error points to a step outside the code, such as a manual exclusion, which must be found before either figure is trusted.
misconceptions: Takes a clean run for a correct one
Trusts the re-run over the report before knowing why they differ
Hides a discrepancy instead of explaining it

questions.prompt: Two runs of the same script give 5.08 and 5.17. Which repository rule prevents this?
options: Pin every package version in a lock file
Use only relative paths
Name every input file and its source in the README
Fix the seed of every random step in the code
questions.explanation: Different results from the same code and data come from randomness; a fixed seed makes the run repeatable.
misconceptions: Versions explain a failure across machines, not two runs on one
Paths make a script fail, not vary
Documentation helps a re-run start; it does not make results repeat

questions.prompt: True or false: a reviewer should read the report first, so that the re-run can focus on the claims that matter.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reading first sets expectations; re-running first tests whether the handed-over repository produces the report at all.
misconceptions: Lets the prose decide what gets checked, which is how a fluent wrong report passes

questions.prompt: An analyst uses the approved assistant on anonymised berth data, keeps the prompts, and re-runs every number, but the board paper has no line saying an assistant was used. Under the rules, what is it?
options: A breach of the disclosure rule
Allowed: the data and the verification were right
Allowed, if the reviewer knew about it
A breach of the data rule
questions.explanation: The disclosure rule asks for a line on the deliverable itself; the board must be told, whatever else was done right.
misconceptions: Treats verification as a substitute for telling the readers
Confuses telling the reviewer with telling the recipients
The data were anonymised and the tool approved, so no data rule was broken

questions.prompt: Which rule can a reviewer check from the files of an analysis?
options: Use the assistant responsibly
Keep a verification record of each assisted number
Be transparent with readers about any use of AI in the work
Protect sensitive data where possible
questions.explanation: A verification record is a file a reviewer can open; the others are intentions with no evidence behind them.
misconceptions: States a value, not an action anyone can see done
Names a principle without saying what shows it was met
Leaves the exception open with 'where possible'

questions.prompt: Why does the unit's rule set include one analysis a quarter done without an assistant?
options: To measure how much time the assistant saves
Because the national guidelines forbid assistants for analysis
To keep the skill needed to check the assistant
To give the reviewers a lighter quarter
questions.explanation: Verification needs the skill the assistant replaces; unaided work keeps it alive.
misconceptions: Turns a skill rule into a productivity study
Overstates the guidelines, which set conditions for use, not a ban
Unaided work is reviewed like any other, so it saves no review time

questions.prompt: A draft names vessel masters and their mobile numbers in a table. Fixing it changes no figure and no recommendation. Under the unit's severity scale, how is it rated?
options: Not a finding: it is the data protection officer's matter
Minor: it is presentation, like a label
Major: personal data is serious but the decision stands
Critical: the output cannot leave the unit as it is
questions.explanation: The scale makes a finding critical when the decision changes or when the output cannot leave the unit; personal data in an output is the second case.
misconceptions: Hands the finding to someone else instead of rating it; the reviewer still blocks the release
Rates by the effect on the numbers only and forgets the clause about release
Invents a middle rating for findings that feel serious but leave the numbers alone

questions.prompt: Fixing one flaw moves an estimated effect from -5.36 hours to -1.37; the draft recommends action only at -2 hours or more. Fixing a second flaw moves it on to -0.94. How do the two flaws rate?
options: First critical, second major
First major, second critical: the second leaves the smaller effect
Both critical: both move the estimate
Both major: neither alone gives the final figure
questions.explanation: The first fix alone takes the effect below the decision threshold, so the decision changes; the second changes the size, not the decision.
misconceptions: Rates by the final figure, not by what each fix does to the decision
Treats any change in the estimate as critical, so the scale stops separating findings
Asks each flaw to explain the whole gap, which no single flaw has to do

questions.prompt: Two reviewers rate the same six findings and differ by two levels on one of them. What should the calibration session produce?
options: An average of the two ratings for that finding
A sentence added to the checklist that would have prevented the gap
A note in the review file that the two reviewers see the finding differently
The senior reviewer's rating, recorded as final
questions.explanation: A large gap shows a checklist item that admits two readings; changing its wording is what makes the next review agree.
misconceptions: Splits the difference, which is right for neither reading
Records the disagreement without changing anything that caused it
Settles one case by seniority and leaves the ambiguity for the next

questions.prompt: An assisted analysis used the approved assistant, re-ran every number and disclosed the use. The data sent to the assistant were the names and shifts of pilots. What does the audit record?
options: No breach: the work was verified and disclosed
A breach of the disclosure rule, since the pilots were never told their data were used
A breach of the data rule; tell the data protection officer and redo on anonymised data
A minor note for the analyst's feedback
questions.explanation: Restricted personal data left the authority's control; verification and disclosure do not undo that, and the officer must be told.
misconceptions: Lets right figures and an honest disclosure excuse what was sent
The use was disclosed; the problem is what the assistant was given
Downgrades a data breach to a development point

questions.prompt: An assisted analysis reports 18.4% and has no verification record. You recompute 47.7% from the authority's data. What action does the audit table record?
options: Correct the figure to 47.7% in the released paper and tell its readers
Ask the analyst to add a verification record
Note it for the next quarter's audit
Withdraw the figure, then re-run and re-review the analysis
questions.explanation: A released figure that the data contradict must be withdrawn; the auditor's recomputation is a check, not a reviewed replacement.
misconceptions: Releases the auditor's own number without the review the original lacked
Adds paperwork to a figure already known to be wrong
Leaves a wrong figure in circulation for a quarter

questions.prompt: An audit of five assisted analyses finds two with no verification record. What is the best change to propose?
options: No review of assisted work starts without its verification record
Warn the two analysts in writing
Ban the assistant until the next audit
Audit every assisted analysis from now on, not a sample of five
questions.explanation: Two of five points at the process: making the record a condition of review catches it every time, before release.
misconceptions: Treats a process gap as two personal failings, which teaches the unit to hide assistant use
Removes a tool the rules already allow with conditions
Multiplies audit hours instead of fixing the step that let the gap through

questions.prompt: A reviewer found seven things in a new analyst's notebook, from a missing comparison group to variable names. How many should the feedback conversation raise?
options: All seven of them, so that nothing is hidden from her
About three that show a pattern in her reasoning
None: send the review notes instead
Only the most severe one
questions.explanation: Three findings that share a reasoning gap are what she can remember and act on; the rest stay in the review notes.
misconceptions: Confuses the review of the analysis with feedback to the person
Notes tell her what was wrong, not how to reason next time
Leaves out patterns she needs to see together

questions.prompt: Which part of a feedback note does most to build an analyst's skill on a new problem?
options: The observation: the cell and the number
The effect of the error on the decision the analysis informed
The reasoning: the question she did not ask herself
The praise that opens the note
questions.explanation: The reasoning line names a question she can ask on any future problem; the other parts are tied to this notebook.
misconceptions: Locates this error but does not carry to the next problem
Shows why it mattered here without saying how to avoid it
Helps the tone but teaches nothing unless it is specific

questions.prompt: A new analyst's lowest skill is verifying assisted work. Why does her three-month plan end with an analysis done without the assistant?
options: To measure how fast she is without it
Because juniors may not use the assistant
To give her reviewer a simpler analysis
She cannot check work she cannot do herself
questions.explanation: Verifying an assistant's output needs the skill it replaces; unaided work builds and shows that skill.
misconceptions: Turns a skill goal into a speed test
The rules allow juniors to use the approved assistant with conditions
Unaided work is reviewed at its normal level

questions.prompt: Level 3 reviews take 10 senior hours and level 4 reviews 16, plus a second reviewer. Next quarter has 12 level 3 and 4 level 4 analyses. How many senior hours do they need?
options: 184 hours
152 hours
120 hours
216 hours
questions.explanation: 12 × 10 + 4 × 16 = 184; the second reviewer's hours need not be a senior's.
misconceptions: Counts level 4 at the level 3 rate
Leaves out the level 4 reviews
Charges the second reviewers' hours to the seniors as well

questions.prompt: A co-signed level 3 review has a mid-level analyst review and a senior check the review in 2 hours, in place of 10. How many co-signed reviews close a senior shortfall of 34 hours?
options: Four
Five
Seventeen
Three
questions.explanation: Each co-signed review saves 8 senior hours; four save 32, short of 34, so five are needed.
misconceptions: Rounds down and leaves the rota 2 hours short
Divides by the 2 co-sign hours instead of the 8 saved
Divides by 10, as if the senior spent nothing on a co-signed review

questions.prompt: True or false: a rota where two seniors end at 100% of their review hours is ready for the quarter.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It keeps every rule but has no slack: an urgent level 3 request has nowhere to go, so the plan should say what moves when one arrives.
misconceptions: Takes a rota that fits on paper for one that survives the quarter

questions.prompt: A level 3 question takes 1.5 analyst days; the unit plans one review day at level 3. The deadline is in two working days and the sponsor asks for it plus a level 2 question of 1 analyst day. What fits?
options: Both, with the level 3 review shortened to half a day
Both: 2.5 analyst days is close enough
The level 3 question alone, with its review
Neither: refuse until a later board
questions.explanation: The level 3 question needs 2.5 days with review; it alone fills the deadline, so the second question becomes an option for later.
misconceptions: Cuts the review the level requires to fit the diary
Sizes the analysis without its review and overruns the deadline
Refuses when an option fits

questions.prompt: At the start of a scoping meeting the sponsor says: "I need the slot-booking result in a week." What is your first move?
options: Offer the two options that fit a week
Agree, and work out the scope afterwards
Explain at once why a week is too short for a level 3 review with its re-run
Ask which decision the result informs and what evidence would convince him
questions.explanation: The decision and the evidence he would accept change which option is best; offering before asking sizes the wrong request.
misconceptions: Offers before knowing what the result is for
Promises a scope nobody has sized
Opens with a refusal before knowing what is needed

questions.prompt: Why does a scope agreement list the questions that are out of scope?
options: So that nobody later assumes the paper answered them
Because the unit's standard limits each paper to two questions
To show the sponsor how much work was refused
To claim the extra analysis days for the next quarter
questions.explanation: Writing what is out, and when it comes, stops readers and the sponsor from taking silence for an answer.
misconceptions: Invents a rule; the limit is the days, not a count of questions
Turns a record into a complaint
Confuses a scope record with capacity planning

questions.prompt: With twelve months of data after a change, the smallest effect the comparison can reliably detect is 0.66 hours. The operations team says the change pays only from 2 hours. Which threshold goes into the agreement?
options: 0.66 hours: the smallest detectable change
2 hours: it matters to the decision and the data can detect it
1 hour, as a compromise between the detectable change and the cost
Any fall at all, as the sponsor first asked
questions.explanation: The threshold comes from the decision (2 hours pays for the scheme); the detectable change only confirms the data can test it.
misconceptions: Takes the data's precision as the decision's threshold
Splits the difference with no reason in the decision
Writes a rule any noise could meet

questions.prompt: When should the analysis agreement, with its decision rule, be signed?
options: After the result, so the rule fits what was found
After a first look at the data, to set a realistic threshold
Before the analysis starts
When the board paper is approved
questions.explanation: A rule signed before the result cannot be bent to it; any later change is dated and signed again.
misconceptions: Fits the rule to the result, which makes it no rule
A first look at the outcome already informs the threshold
Signs it when it can no longer guide anything

questions.prompt: An agreed rule says: extend if waiting falls by at least 2 hours and no vessel type waits more than 2 hours longer. The result: a fall of 0.78 hours overall; feeders wait 6.32 hours longer. What does the rule say?
options: Extend: waiting fell overall
Extend to all terminals except for feeders
Re-run with a longer window until it passes
Do not extend as it is: both conditions fail
questions.explanation: The fall is below 2 hours and one type loses more than 2 hours; the rule's alternative applies: keep at T2 and fix the feeder slots.
misconceptions: Reads the sign of the effect and ignores the threshold
Invents a partial option the agreement does not contain
Changes the data window after seeing the result

questions.prompt: A director writes: "The subgroup table is based on very few cases; please check it before the board." Is this pressure or a challenge?
options: A challenge: it questions whether the finding is sound, and can be checked
Pressure: any request from a sponsor about a finding is pressure on it, whatever it says
Pressure, because it comes from a director
Neither: subgroup tables are optional
questions.explanation: It questions the evidence, not its visibility; recompute and report the count, and the finding may change.
misconceptions: Treats every question as an attack, which shuts out fair corrections
Judges the request by rank instead of content
Treats a finding the rule depends on as decoration

questions.prompt: You decide to keep a subgroup result a senior asked you to remove. What must the decision record contain?
options: The decision only, so that the record stays short and easy to read
The request, the checked finding, the options, the decision, its reasons and the rules cited
The request and the senior's name, sent to the chief executive at once
The finding with its statistical test, the count of cases and the analyst who checked it
questions.explanation: Someone who was not there must see why: what was asked, what was checked, what was weighed and on what rules.
misconceptions: Leaves the reasons out, so the decision cannot be defended later
Makes the record about a person, not the decision
Records the evidence but not the decision taken on it

questions.prompt: Which reply best keeps both the finding and the working relationship with the senior who asked to remove it?
options: The table stays: removing findings would breach our ethics and our standard, as you know
I will remove it once you put the request in writing to the unit
I see the concern; the agreed rule needs the table, so it stays, with context and your plan
As you prefer: I will move it to an appendix at the back of the paper
questions.explanation: It acknowledges him, keeps the finding on the rule he agreed to, and gives him something to add rather than lose.
misconceptions: Right decision, but lectures and gives him nothing to do
Trades the finding for paperwork
Hides the finding while appearing to keep it

questions.prompt: Which sentence belongs in a board quality statement about uncertainty?
options: Results should be interpreted with appropriate caution given the limitations of the data used
Uncertainty was assessed by the review team
The analysis used robust statistical methods
The fall is likely between 0.3 and 1.3 hours per call, below the agreed 2 hours
questions.explanation: A range set beside the agreed threshold lets the board weigh the result without the method.
misconceptions: Warns without saying how much
Says uncertainty was looked at, not what it is
Describes the method, not what remains uncertain

questions.prompt: A released quarterly figure was understated because two weeks of an extract were loaded twice. What does the correction notice give as the cause?
options: A load that accepted duplicated weeks, and no duplicate check
An unexplained data issue
The analyst who ran the quarterly figure
The vendor of the terminal system, which re-sent the two weeks
questions.explanation: The notice names the cause in the process and the change that prevents it, so the next error gets reported.
misconceptions: Gives no cause, so no process changes
Blames a person, which teaches the unit to hide errors
Moves the blame outside and leaves the unit's missing check in place

questions.prompt: True or false: a released figure that turns out to be too low, and so understated the authority's performance, needs no correction notice.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The figure left the authority and others used it; whatever the direction of the error, they are told.
misconceptions: Lets the direction of the error decide whether readers are told
